tier_reason: results/results-avx-2.csv has an MKL CSR column beside the four SPC5 kernels, and the README labels it 'results for the paper & avx512', i.e. the data of the peer-reviewed SPC5 SVE/AVX-512 paper (Regnault and Bramas, Computer Science and Information Systems 21(1):203-221, 2024, per search results; comsis.org is blocked so the paper was not opened). Code (load_mm_and_compare, jobs-plafrim.sh), g++ 11.2.0, MKL 2022.0.2 and CMake flags are public, but no exact CPU model is given, so not A.

corrections.claimed_speedup: From results/results-avx-2.csv, taking the best of the four SPC5 sequential kernels per matrix against the MKL CSR column, rows without manual horizontal sum (derived from page data): median 1.23x in double and 1.49x in float, geometric mean 1.18x and 1.45x, SPC5 ahead on 16 of 23 matrices in double and 17 of 23 in float, up to 1.90x (double) and 3.00x (float), but slower on others (worst 0.45x double, 0.41x float). The MHSUM=ON build gives similar figures (double median 1.24x, float median 1.64x, max 3.12x).
corrections.caveats: The best kernel is picked per matrix after the fact, which flatters SPC5 (the library ships a performance predictor, but the ratios above use the measured best). The CSV has an MKL column only for sequential runs; parallel SPC5 columns have no MKL counterpart. Conversion is costly: on CO (double) the raw log shows SPC5 conversion of 0.39-0.46 s against 0.09 s for MKL CSR, while 16 timed SpMVs take 0.13-0.19 s, so a conversion costs roughly 40-55 SpMVs (derived from page data), and MKL (1.89 GFlop/s) beats the best SPC5 kernel (1.70) on that matrix. The CSV is the 2023 data of the 2024 ComSIS paper, not the 2018 PeerJ CS paper. CPU class only (PlaFRIM bora Cascade Lake nodes), no model. The GitHub repo is a mirror of gitlab.inria.fr/bramas/spc5, which could not be checked (blocked), so the official repo may be newer than the mirror's 2023-07-25 last commit.

notes: Recomputed every ratio from the CSV (92 rows: 23 matrices x double/float x hsum yes/no) and they match the record. Repo page: MIT, 6 stars, 2 forks, 108 commits, mirror of the Inria GitLab; latest commit 2023-07-25 ('update readme'). The tier stays B because the CSV is the data of a peer-reviewed 2024 paper, not because of the 2018 PeerJ paper.

tier_reason: The README's KLU averages are first-party and doc/results(version202205).pdf adds first-party charts with partial methodology (gcc 4.8.5 without flags, Intel Xeon Gold 6130 16-core, KLU 1.3.9, NICSLU 202110, MKL PARDISO 2022.0.2, 66 SuiteSparse circuit matrices); the solver is closed-source binaries and no harness is published, so C. The IEEE TCAD 2025 paper could not be opened (dl.acm.org and arxiv.org blocked) and search results did not show its abstract numbers.

corrections.claimed_speedup: README: on average more than 3X faster than KLU when sequential and more than 25X faster with 16 threads (66 SuiteSparse circuit matrices, KLU with approximate minimum degree ordering). doc/results(version202205).pdf, read from line charts (approximate): average factorization speedup about 2.8x over KLU at 1 thread and about 14.6x at 16 threads, about 9.8-10.5x over MKL PARDISO and 1.2-5.2x over NICSLU at 1-16 threads; re-factorization about 1.7x and 10.6x over KLU, about 12.3-14.1x over MKL PARDISO, about 1.2-1.4x over NICSLU; solving about 1.05-2.1x over KLU and 3.2-3.7x over MKL PARDISO. In that PDF KLU uses NICSLU's ordering rather than AMD, which lowers the KLU ratios.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: gcc 4.8.5 on CentOS 7.9 for the version-202205 comparison PDF; flags not stated; prebuilt binaries are shipped per platform (centos6 gcc482, centos7 gcc485, rocky8 gcc850, win7)
corrections.hardware: Intel Xeon Gold 6130 (16 cores, 2.1 GHz), 256 GB RAM (doc/results(version202205).pdf); README averages give no hardware
corrections.license: Proprietary freeware binaries with no license text; the library requires a signed key file (license/cktso.lic) whose EXPIRE field is 2028-12-31
corrections.caveats: Binary-only: the repository ships compiled libraries, a header, demos and docs, not source, so it cannot be audited or copied. The library needs license/cktso.lic, a signed key file with EXPIRE = 2028-12-31, so a pinned binary can stop working when the key expires. The README averages (>3x, >25x) are first-party without hardware or method; the 2022 PDF is from an old version ('results are from an old version') and shows lower KLU ratios (about 2.8x and 14.6x), in part because KLU there used NICSLU's ordering. Its scatter plots show MKL PARDISO factorizing several of the largest matrices (over 1M rows) faster than CKTSO, so the averages hide losses on big cases. The GPU-solver comparisons reuse numbers from other papers rather than running those solvers. The IEEE TCAD 2025 paper was not opened.

notes: Opened the results PDF (rendered pages 1-4) and the license directory: no licence text, only a readme and a signed key file with an expiry date (shortcoming worth recording). Repo page: 47 stars, 8 forks, 88 commits, not a fork; latest commit 2026-03-26 ('20260321').

tier_reason: Upgraded from C. GraphBLAST's own paper is peer-reviewed in ACM Transactions on Mathematical Software (doi 10.1145/3466795, per several search results; the README cites the arXiv preprint 1908.01407), and its abstract as quoted in search results gives 43.51x geometric-mean and 1268x peak speedup over multi-threaded SuiteSparse GraphBLAS. The paper could not be opened (dl.acm.org, arxiv.org and par.nsf.gov are blocked), so B rests on the venue plus the abstract, per earlier precedents; the spla README chart is third-party secondary evidence without flags.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Peer-reviewed ACM TOMS paper (Yang, Buluc, Owens, 'GraphBLAST: A High-Performance Linear Algebra-based Graph Framework on the GPU', doi 10.1145/3466795), per its abstract as quoted in search results: 43.51x geometric mean and 1268x peak speedup over SuiteSparse GraphBLAS on multi-threaded CPUs, and on average at least an order of magnitude over SuiteSparse and GBTL. Third-party check in the spla README chart (docs/stats/rq1_rel.png, log scale, GTX 1070 against LAGraph on a 4-core i7-6700, read by eye): PageRank roughly 13x to 75x, triangle counting roughly 5x to 13x, BFS roughly 0.4x to 4.5x and SSSP roughly 0.2x to 2.6x (slower than LAGraph on some graphs).
corrections.workload: BFS, SSSP, PageRank and triangle counting on graph adjacency matrices; GraphBLAST on one NVIDIA GPU against SuiteSparse:GraphBLAS (directly in the paper; through LAGraph in the spla chart) on a multi-core CPU.
corrections.caveats: GPU against CPU in both sources, so not like for like; the paper's numbers were seen only as an abstract quote in search results (paper blocked), so its GPU, CPU, SuiteSparse version, compiler and flags are unverified, and the 43.51x geometric mean is an aggregate over its own algorithm and graph mix. In the spla chart (made by a competing project, no flags or harness for GraphBLAST in the repo) GraphBLAST has no bar for comOrkut and i2004 in BFS/SSSP and none for comOrkut, socLvJr, rggn223s0 and rdcent in PageRank, which suggests it failed or was not run on those larger graphs on the 8 GB GPU; it is slower than LAGraph on several BFS and SSSP graphs. Last commit 2021-06-18; CUDA build era of 2019-2021.

notes: The record's ranges match my reading of rq1_rel.png (PageRank top is GraphBLAST's citPat bar, around 75x; the axis has only one labelled tick, so it is approximate). The record called the paper 'TOPC'; search results place it in ACM TOMS. Repo page: Apache-2.0, 238 stars, 28 forks, not archived, 532 commits; latest commit 2021-06-18.
